Leah · Genesis 29:21-30

When Men Treat You as a Commodity

From The God Who Hears Her by Dr. Connie Champeon · 4 min read

“Then Jacob said to Laban, “Give me my wife, for my time is completed, that I may go in to her.” Laban gathered all the men of the place and made a feast. Now in the evening he took his daughter Leah, and brought her to him; and Jacob went in to her. Laban also gave his maid Zilpah to his daughter Leah as a maid. So it came about in the morning that, behold, it was Leah! And he said to Laban, “What is this you have done to me? Was it not for Rachel that I served with you? Why then have you deceived me?” But Laban said, “It is not the practice in our place to marry off the younger before the firstborn. Complete the week of this one, and we will give you the other also for the service which you shall serve with me for another seven years.” Jacob did so and completed her week, and he gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife. Laban also gave his maid Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her maid. So Jacob went in to Rachel also, and indeed he loved Rachel more than Leah, and he served with Laban for another seven years.” (Genesis 29:21-30)

Laban treated both of his daughters as commodities to get what he wanted. Later the women say this "Does he not regard us as foreigners? Not only has he sold us, but he has used up what was paid for us" (Gen 31:15). Jacob did not treat them much better. Both sisters missed out in this contract. Jacob bought them with his strength and diligent labor; they were treated as property and not even given a dowry like Rebekah had been given. Both of them were robbed of the rights of a wife. Leah only had Jacob for 7 days before she had to share him for decades. Rachel did not get a public wedding feast; she was simply an add-on to Leah’s. Leah got the honor of being the first wife, but she did not have Jacob’s love and allegiance.

ANE women did not wear veils or robes. Remember Genesis 29:17, “Rachel was beautiful in form.” Jacob could see her form, and she was a 10 out of 10, she knocked his 77-year-old sandals off. So how could he mistake her for Leah? Do you remember how Rebekah put on a veil when she met Isaac? Veils were part of the wedding ceremony. Tents were very dark with no windows. Plus, despite the discomfort it gives many believers, Jacob would have been pretty drunk that far into the wedding feast. That is what happened during a wedding feast. Otherwise, he would have felt it wasn’t Leah even if he couldn’t see the difference. But for this deception to happen, both daughters had to consent to it, although neither of them would have had much choice. If Leah refused, she would have faced severe social consequences; likely her father would have refused to arrange for her to marry anyone else, and she would have been publicly shamed. Rachel did not speak up. At any point she could have made sure Jacob saw her, and the deceit would have been revealed. But this would have been at the cost of publicly defying her father and destroying her sister's only chance at marriage. These women were caught in a culture where their father held all the power, and he abused it and them.

Jacob had stolen the blessing, deceiving his blind and nearly deaf father. Now Laban was doing the same thing to Jacob when his senses were dull and he couldn't see. Laban was a bad dad and an awful person in general. Part of the bride price should have gone to Rachel and Leah’s dowries. Jacob made Laban a very rich man, but instead of using those funds to provide for his daughters’ future like he should have and was custom, he used it only to enrich himself and his sons. Daughters had certain rights and expectations of protection from their fathers and clans. By keeping everything he gained, Laban treated his daughters as slaves to be sold for his personal benefit. He didn’t treat them as members of the clan; he liquidated them to expand his own flock. Laban is the ultimate deceiver and user, and his daughters pay the highest price.

What should women do when they are part of a broken system that uses and abuses them? When Leah and Rachel get a chance, they escape, but that will take another 20 years. It will take 20 years for them to find a way out. For twenty years, they are trapped knowing they are being sacrificed and having no power to stop it. There’s twenty years of constantly trying to please a father who will never be pleased. He may consume all their financial inheritance, but he can’t touch their spiritual or genetic legacy. They are the matriarchs of the 12 tribes with no help or credit to their father. There are lessons here on both sides. I need to be careful that I’m not Laban, using people to accomplish “a greater agenda.” The mission is always about the people, the ones serving with me as much as the ones we are trying to serve. God never blesses treating people as expendable or inferior. I also need to know the difference between when I’m being sacrificial for a worthy cause and when I’m being sacrificed for someone’s ego or agenda. Leah and Rachel struggled with trying to please their father, I know a lot of women do. I had a great dad, so that’s not my struggle. Mine is feeling that I need to fix everything and that if it falls apart it’s my fault. Neither lie is true. Through all the brokenness of this family, God is at work building a nation and a kingdom. He doesn’t need perfect families, He needs willing ones.

(NASB)
